claim: Cooperators who pay a cost to produce publically-available benefits can be exploited by cheaters who do not contribute fairly.
source: Cooperators who pay a cost to produce publically-available benefits can be exploited by cheaters who do not contribute fairly.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in cooperation theory, drawing from established scientific consensus in evolutionary biology.

claim: Two classes of mechanisms are known to promote cooperation: 'partner choice' and 'partner fidelity feedback'.
source: Two classes of mechanisms are known to promote cooperation: 'partner choice', where a cooperator preferentially interacts with cooperative over cheating partners; and 'partner fidelity feedback', where repeated interactions between individuals ensure that cheaters suffer as their cooperative partners languish (see, for example, Momeni et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Momeni et al., 2013 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Partner fidelity feedback at sub-organismal level can appear as partner choice at organismal level.
source: Here, I resolve this controversy by noting that selection can operate on organismal and sub-organismal 'entities' such that partner fidelity feedback at sub-organismal level can appear as partner choice at organismal level.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference presented as the main contribution of the manuscript.

claim: Cooperation between multicellular eukaryotes and mitochondria is promoted by partner fidelity feedback and partner choice between sub-organismal entities.
source: I also show that cooperation between multicellular eukaryotes and mitochondria is promoted by partner fidelity feedback and partner choice between sub-organismal entities, in addition to being promoted by partner fidelity feedback between hosts and symbionts, as was previously known.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference and analysis presented in the manuscript, building on established knowledge.

claim: Cooperation is thought to drive major evolutionary transitions such as the emergence of eukaryotes and multicellularity.
source: Cooperation is thought to drive major evolutionary transitions such as the emergence of eukaryotes and multicellularity (Maynard Smith and Szathmary, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maynard Smith and Szathmary, 1998.

claim: Cooperation between pathogenic microbes can worsen microbial infection.
source: Cooperation between pathogenic microbes can worsen microbial infection (Sandoz et al., 2007; Falsetta et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sandoz et al., 2007 and Falsetta et al., 2014.

claim: Cooperation between cells in tumor microenvironment can hasten cancer progression.
source: Cooperation between cells in tumor microenvironment can hasten cancer progression (Rattigan et al., 2012; Cleary et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rattigan et al., 2012 and Cleary et al., 2014.

claim: Cooperation may persist only if the community is partitioned into interaction groups that are sufficiently variable in cooperator frequency.
source: In this case, cooperation may persist only if the community is partitioned into interaction groups (groups) (Appendix note 6) that are sufficiently variable in cooperator frequency (Price, 1970; Trivers, 1971; Bull and Rice, 1991; Frank, 1994; 1997; Foster and Wenseleers, 2006; Fletcher and Doebeli, 2009) (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Cooperator frequency can increase in a community despite decreasing in each group when cooperator-dominated groups produce more cooperative benefits than cheater-dominated groups.
source: This way, since cooperator-dominated groups will produce more cooperative benefits than cheater-dominated groups, individuals in cooperator-dominated groups (likely cooperators) will reproduce more than individuals in cheater-dominated groups (likely cheaters). Consequently, cooperator frequency can increase in a community despite decreasing in each group (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a theoretical inference based on the Price equation framework, illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: During iron limitation, cooperative Pseudomonas aeruginosa cells pay a fitness cost to synthesize siderophores which are released into the environment to scavenge iron.
source: During iron limitation, a focal cooperative Pseudomonas aeruginosa cell (grey filled oval) pays a fitness cost to synthesize siderophores (grey triangles, color indicating origin) which are released into the environment to scavenge iron.
evidence: This is an example described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Cheating Pseudomonas aeruginosa cells use siderophores without contributing any and are competitively superior to cooperators.
source: In contrast, a cheating partner (blue unfilled oval) uses siderophores without contributing any, and is competitively superior to cooperators (Griffin et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Griffin et al., 2004.

claim: A focal client fish will preferentially visit a cleaner fish if the cleaner previously cooperated with instead of cheated another client.
source: A focal client (grey, bottom) will preferentially visit a cleaner (smaller blue fish) if the cleaner previously cooperated with (filled blue) instead of cheated (unfilled blue) another client (yellow, top) (Bshary and Grutter, 2006) or the focal client itself (grey, top) (Bshary and Schäffer, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bshary and Grutter, 2006 and Bshary and Schäffer, 2002.

claim: Cooperative yeast cells expressing cell surface adhesive proteins bind better to other adhesive cooperators than to non-adhesive cheaters.
source: A focal cooperative yeast cell (grey) pays a fitness cost to express cell surface adhesive proteins. The focal adhesive cell will bind better to other adhesive cooperators (filled blue) than to non-adhesive cheaters (unfilled blue). This differential binding (solid versus dashed grey box) favors cooperation between adhesive cells, and allows the formation of cell clumps with enhanced stress resistance (Smukalla et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smukalla et al., 2008.

claim: Vertical transmission of mitochondria ensures that mitochondria will harm their own fitness if they do not serve their host.
source: However, vertical transmission of mitochondria means that host and mitochondria repeatedly interact with each other. This ensures that mitochondria will harm their own fitness if they do not serve their host (compare left with right).
evidence: This is an inference based on the logic of partner fidelity feedback in the context of vertical transmission.

claim: Cooperative mitochondria can persist if their frequency varies greatly among different hosts.
source: Consequently, cooperative mitochondria can persist (compare bottom with top) if their frequency varies greatly among different hosts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Price equation framework applied to mitochondrial cooperation.

claim: The framework by Sachs et al. classifies pro-cooperation mechanisms to either 'partner choice (PC)' or 'partner fidelity feedback (PFF)'.
source: Several conceptual frameworks have attempted to classify pro-cooperation mechanisms (Sachs et al., 2004; Nowak, 2006; Lehmann and Keller, 2006; West et al., 2007). Unlike most frameworks which focus on kin cooperation, the framework by Sachs et al. considers both kin and mutualistic cooperation. It classifies pro-cooperation mechanisms known under a plethora of names ('kin selection', 'host sanctioning/policing', 'green beard', 'reciprocity' - to name a few) to either 'partner choice (PC)' or 'partner fidelity feedback (PFF)' (Sachs et al., 2004) (Appendix note 7).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sachs et al., 2004.

claim: In partner choice, a focal cooperator 'recognizes' and 'chooses' cooperative instead of cheating partners to interact with.
source: In PC, a focal cooperator 'recognizes' and 'chooses' cooperative instead of cheating partners to interact with.
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge from Sachs et al., 2004.

claim: Partner choice can occur before or after interacting with partners ('conditional response').
source: Choice can occur before (Figure 1C,i) or after (Figure 1C,ii) interacting with partners ('conditional response') (Sachs et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sachs et al., 2004 and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Archetti et al. has broadened partner choice to include 'screening' where a focal individual displays a single fixed response that favors cooperative over cheating partners.
source: Archetti et al. has broadened PC to include 'screening' where a focal individual displays a single fixed response, but this response favors cooperative over cheating partners (Archetti et al., 2011a; 2011b) (Figure 1C,iii; Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by citations to Archetti et al., 2011a and 2011b.

claim: Partner choice causes cooperator frequency to vary among groups as a focal cooperator favors cooperative over cheating partners.
source: Thus, PC causes cooperator frequency to vary among groups as a focal cooperator favors cooperative over cheating partners during (Figure 1C) or after (Figure 3D) the formation of interaction groups.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of partner choice.

claim: In partner fidelity feedback, individuals are associated for an extended series of exchanges that last long enough that a feedback operates.
source: In PFF, individuals are "associated for an extended series of exchanges that last long enough that a feedback operates" (Sachs et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a direct quote from Sachs et al., 2004.

claim: During repeated interactions, an individual who does not help its cooperative partner will eventually suffer because its cooperative partner suffers or even dies.
source: That is, during repeated interactions (e.g. in a spatially-structured environment), an individual who does not help its cooperative partner will eventually suffer because its cooperative partner suffers (Figure 1D) or even dies.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of partner fidelity feedback, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: In partner fidelity feedback, high inter-group variability in cooperator frequency can be achieved via population bottlenecks.
source: In PFF, high inter-group variability in cooperator frequency, which is required for promoting cooperation, can be achieved via population bottlenecks (drastic reductions in population sizes) (Brockhurst and Svensson, 2007; Chuang et al., 2009; Nadell et al., 2010; Harcombe, 2010; Van Dyken et al., 2013; Datta et al., 2013; van Gestel et al., 2014; Waite et al., 2015) (Appendix note 8).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Population bottlenecks can be realized through range expansion of a few individuals to new locations.
source: Population bottlenecks can be realized through range expansion of a few individuals to new locations (Hallatschek et al., 2007; Mitri et al., 2015, population dilutions (Chuang et al., 2009), population crashes caused by cheaters (Waite et al., 2015), and selection for rare adaptive mutants (Morgan et al., 2012; Waite and Shou, 2012; Asfahl et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hallatschek et al., 2007 and Mitri et al., 2015.

claim: Partner choice can lead to partner fidelity feedback.
source: However, PC can lead to PFF (e.g. a client fish returning again and again to the same cooperative cleaner fish [(Bshary and Schäffer, 2002]), thus blurring the distinction between PC and PFF.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bshary and Schäffer, 2002 as an example.

claim: Sachs et al. suggested that unlike partner choice, partner fidelity feedback is 'automatic', 'passive', and 'does not require recognition or conditional response'.
source: Sachs et al. and other further suggested that unlike PC, PFF is 'automatic', 'passive', and 'does not require recognition or conditional response' (Sachs et al., 2004; Foster and Wenseleers, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sachs et al., 2004 and Foster and Wenseleers, 2006.

claim: On an agarose pad lacking adenine and lysine supplements, [A− L+] and [L− A+] physically associate with each other and grow tall while [L−] fail to grow tall.
source: On an agarose pad lacking adenine and lysine supplements, [A− L+] (green) and its cooperative [L− A+] (magenta) and cheating [L−] (blue) partners undergo self-organization from an initially random spatial distribution. [A− L+] and [L− A+] physically associate with each other and grow tall. [L−], isolated from [A− L+], fail to grow tall.
evidence: This is experimental data from Momeni et al., 2013, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Disruption of repeated interactions via frequent mixing favors cheater [L−] over cooperator [L− A+].
source: Consistent with this being PFF, disruption of repeated interactions via frequent mixing favors cheater [L−] over cooperator [L− A+].
evidence: This is experimental data from Momeni et al., 2013.

claim: Population bottleneck during spatial range expansion favors cooperator [L− A+] over cheater [L−].
source: Furthermore, population bottleneck during spatial range expansion (Hallatschek et al., 2007; Mitri et al., 2015), which presumably increases variability in cooperator frequency across different locations, favors cooperator (L− A+] over cheater (L−] (Momeni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is experimental data from Momeni et al., 2013, with citations to Hallatschek et al., 2007 and Mitri et al., 2015 for the concept of spatial range expansion.

claim: Mutualisms between fig trees and fig wasps have been thought to be stabilized by partner choice by some authors and partner fidelity feedback by others.
source: In fact, mutualisms such as those between fig trees and fig wasps (Jander and Herre, 2010), between yuccas and yucca moths (Pellmyr and Huth, 1994), and between legumes and rhizobia (Kiers et al., 2003) have been thought to be stabilized by PC by some authors (Sachs et al., 2004; Kiers et al., 2011) and PFF by other (Archetti et al., 2011a; Weyl et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes a controversy in the literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: In yucca-yucca moth mutualisms, a yucca selectively aborts flowers dominated by cheating pollinator offspring.
source: For example, in yucca-yucca moth mutualisms, a yucca selectively aborts flowers dominated by cheating pollinator offspring (Pellmyr and Huth, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pellmyr and Huth, 1994.

claim: The partner choice camp argues that a yucca plant partitions its resource into separate flowers and 'decides' whether a flower has enough cheating pollinators to be aborted.
source: The PC camp argues that a plant partitions its resource into separate flowers, and 'decides' whether a flower has enough cheating pollinators to be aborted (Sachs et al., 2004).
evidence: This represents an interpretation from Sachs et al., 2004.

claim: The partner fidelity feedback camp counters that flower abortion is the fitness consequence of being damaged by cheating pollinators during excessive oviposition.
source: The PFF camp counters that flower abortion is not PC, but rather the fitness consequence of being damaged by cheating pollinators during excessive oviposition, since experimentally-inflicted damages also trigger flower abortion (Weyl et al., 2010; Archetti et al., 2011a; Weyl et al., 2011).
evidence: This represents an interpretation from Weyl et al., 2010, Archetti et al., 2011a, and Weyl et al., 2011.

claim: An alternative criterion for distinguishing partner fidelity feedback and partner choice has been proposed: If an individual's response is specific to the cheating behavior of a partner, then partner choice operates; if the response is toward general stress, then partner fidelity feedback operates.
source: This controversy has led to the proposal of an alternative criterion for distinguishing PFF and PC: If an individual's response is specific to the cheating behavior of a partner, then PC operates; if the response is toward general stress (which may or may not be inflicted by a cheating partner), then PFF operates (Archetti et al., 2011a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Archetti et al., 2011a.

claim: A biological entity is a biological structure with a boundary such that the birth, or growth, or survival, or death of an entity is separable from that of other similar entities.
source: A biological entity (entity) is a biological structure with a boundary such that the birth, or growth, or survival, or death of an entity is separable from that of other similar entities due to chemical or physical coupling within an entity and the lack of equivalent coupling between entities (Appendix note 11).
evidence: This is a definition proposed by the author.

claim: A yucca is an entity because different parts of the yucca are coupled physically and chemically.
source: An organism such as a yucca is an entity, because different parts of the yucca are coupled not only physically but also chemically (e.g. metabolism), and because equivalent intra-yucca coupling does not exist between yuccas.
evidence: This is an inference applying the entity definition to a specific example.

claim: A yucca and its internal moth offspring together can be considered an entity.
source: Ascending above organism, an entity can be a collection of organisms. For example, a yucca and its internal moth offspring together can be considered an entity (Appendix note 13). This is because moth offspring depend on host yucca for survival, and this dependency does not extend to another yucca.
evidence: This is an inference applying the entity definition to a specific example.

claim: A yucca flower is an entity because it can be aborted independently of other flowers.
source: Descending below organism, an entity can also be an organismal part. For example, a yucca flower is an entity because it can be aborted independently of other flowers.
evidence: This is an inference applying the entity definition to a specific example.

claim: Mitochondria are entities in a cell, and mitochondrial genomes (mtDNAs) are independently replicating entities in a mitochondrion.
source: Similarly, mitochondria are entities in a cell, and mitochondrial genomes (mtDNAs) are independently replicating entities in a mitochondrion (see section below).
evidence: This is an inference applying the entity definition to mitochondria and mtDNAs.

claim: Partner choice requires that a focal cooperative entity can direct more cooperative benefits to cooperative over cheating partner entities despite their spatial equivalence.
source: PC requires that a focal cooperative entity can direct more cooperative benefits to cooperative over cheating partner entities despite their spatial equivalence (Appendix note 15) (Figure 3B left, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a revised definition proposed by the author.

claim: Partner entities are spatially-equivalent to a focal entity if the focal entity would have interacted with partner entities equally had they been identical.
source: To a focal entity, partner entities are spatially-equivalent if the focal entity would have interacted with partner entities equally had they been identical.
evidence: This is a definition proposed by the author.

claim: Partner fidelity feedback requires the formation of interaction groups that vary significantly in cooperator frequency due to stochasticity and that last long enough so that cooperators benefit from their cooperative acts.
source: PFF requires the formation of interaction groups that vary significantly in cooperator frequency due to stochasticity and that last long enough so that cooperators benefit from their cooperative acts (Figure 3B right, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a revised definition proposed by the author.

claim: Partner choice and partner fidelity feedback can act synergistically.
source: PC and PFF can act synergistically, an idea compatible with existing mathematical framework (e.g. Eq. 1a in [Foster and Wenseleers, 2006]) and can be found in the anti-competition cooperation among bacteria (Figure 3D) (Chao and Levin, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to Foster and Wenseleers, 2006 and Chao and Levin, 1981, and illustrated in Figure 3D.

claim: Selection against cheating pollinators can occur via partner choice between a focal yucca and its internal pollinator offspring.
source: We now return to the cooperation between yuccas and yucca moths. Selection against cheating pollinators can occur via PC between a focal yucca and its internal pollinator offspring (Figure 3E, left). This is because despite the spatial equivalence of pollinator offspring (i.e. all in the yucca), the focal yucca can selectively abort flowers dominated by cheating pollinator offspring.
evidence: This is an inference applying the revised definitions to the yucca-moth system.

claim: Selection against cheating pollinators can be viewed as partner fidelity feedback between yucca flowers and pollinator offspring.
source: However, we can also view this as PFF between yucca flowers and pollinator offspring (Figure 3E, right). Note that since a focal flower can not discriminate its internal, spatially-equivalent pollinator offspring, PC does not operate here. Instead, PFF between flowers and pollinator offspring requires the spatially-structured environment defined by flowers (Appendix note 19).
evidence: This is an inference applying the revised definitions to the yucca-moth system.

claim: A single mechanism (aborting cheater-dominated flowers) can be viewed as partner choice between a focal yucca and its internal pollinator offspring and as partner fidelity feedback between yucca flowers and pollinator offspring.
source: In summary, a single mechanism (aborting cheater-dominated flowers) can be viewed as PC between a focal yucca and its internal pollinator offspring and as PFF between yucca flowers and pollinator offspring.
evidence: This is a synthesis inference from the analysis of the yucca-moth system.

claim: Partner fidelity feedback at lower levels can appear as partner choice at higher levels.
source: At the same time, since PFF at lower levels (e.g. between yucca flowers and moth offspring) can appear as PC at higher levels (e.g. between a focal yucca and moth offspring) (Figure 3E), we should avoid double-counting.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of multi-level selection.

claim: A cooperative mitochondrial genome harbors genes that are necessary for the host eukaryote, but the transcription of these genes can slow down the replication of mtDNA itself.
source: A cooperative mitochondrial genome (mtDNA) harbors genes that are necessary for the host eukaryote, but the transcription of these genes can slow down the replication of mtDNA itself because these two processes compete for the same protein factor(s) (Larsson et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Larsson et al., 1998.

claim: mtDNAs not performing host-serving functions can gain an advantage in self-replication compared to normal mtDNAs.
source: Thus, mtDNAs not performing host-serving functions can (Hofhaus and Gattermann, 1999; Taylor et al., 2002; Harrison et al., 2014; Jasmin and Zeyl, 2014) (Appendix note 21), though not always (Appendix note 22), gain an advantage in self-replication compared to normal mtDNAs.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hofhaus and Gattermann, 1999; Taylor et al., 2002; Harrison et al., 2014; and Jasmin and Zeyl, 2014.

claim: Dysfunctional mtDNAs can be devastating to the host eukaryote.
source: Dysfunctional mtDNAs can be devastating to the host eukaryote (Chinnery et al., 2000; Chan, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chinnery et al., 2000 and Chan, 2006.

claim: During Drosophila melanogaster oogenesis, mitochondria dominated by functional mtDNAs proliferate faster than mitochondria dominated by dysfunctional mtDNAs.
source: Indeed, during Drosophila melanogaster oogenesis (Hill et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2014), mitochondria dominated by functional mtDNAs proliferate faster than mitochondria dominated by dysfunctional mtDNAs (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hill et al., 2014 and Ma et al., 2014, and illustrated in Figure 4C.

claim: To be transported into the developing oocyte, mitochondria from the surrounding nurse cells need to be localized to the cytoplasmic bridge connecting nurse cells to the oocyte, which depends on mitochondrial function.
source: An example of PC can be found between an oocyte and spatially-equivalent nurse cell mitochondria during D. melanogaster oogenesis: To be transported into the developing oocyte, mitochondria from the surrounding nurse cells need to be localized to the cytoplasmic bridge connecting nurse cells to the oocyte, which in turn depends on mitochondrial function (Cox and Spradling, 2003; Hill et al., 2014) (Figure 4D, left).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cox and Spradling, 2003 and Hill et al., 2014.

claim: During cell division, the stem daughter cell or the young daughter cell preferentially inherits young (functional) mitochondria.
source: A second example can be found during cell division when the stem daughter cell or the young daughter cell preferentially inherits young (functional) mitochondria (McFaline-Figueroa et al., 2011; Katajisto et al., 2015), despite the spatial equivalence of mitochondria in the mother cell (Figure 4D, center).
evidence: Supported by citations to McFaline-Figueroa et al., 2011 and Katajisto et al., 2015.

claim: A host cell uses mitophagy to selectively eliminate dysfunctional mitochondria while retaining functional mitochondria.
source: A third example of PC is a host cell using mitophagy, cellular digestion of mitochondria, to selectively eliminate dysfunctional mitochondria while retaining functional mitochondria (Kim and Lemasters, 2011; Ashrafi and Schwarz, 2013) (Figure 4D, right) (Appendix note 26).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim and Lemasters, 2011 and Ashrafi and Schwarz, 2013.

claim: Mitophagy is active in fertilized oocytes to eliminate paternal mitochondria.
source: Mitophagy-mediated elimination of dysfunctional mtDNAs/mitochondria can conceivably operate in germ cells, given that mitophagy is active in fertilized oocytes to eliminate paternal mitochondria (Ashrafi and Schwarz, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ashrafi and Schwarz, 2013.

claim: In at least several types of mammalian cells, certain mutations in mtDNA will lead host cells to undergo programmed cell death (apoptosis).
source: For example, in at least several types of mammalian cells, certain mutations in mtDNA will lead host cells to undergo programmed cell death (apoptosis) (Zamzami et al., 1995; Chomyn and Attardi, 2003) or cell cycle arrest (Arnould et al., 2002; Owusu-Ansah et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zamzami et al., 1995 and Chomyn and Attardi, 2003.

claim: In birds and mammals, the majority of oocytes die via apoptosis, which has been hypothesized as a mechanism to purge dysfunctional mtDNAs/mitochondria.
source: For example, in birds and mammals, the majority of oocytes die via apoptosis, which has been hypothesized as a mechanism to purge dysfunctional mtDNAs/mitochondria (Krakauer and Mira, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krakauer and Mira, 1999.

claim: Oocytes harboring dysfunctional mtDNAs/mitochondria are less likely to be fertilized.
source: Furthermore, oocytes harboring dysfunctional mtDNAs/mitochondria are less likely to be fertilized (Perez et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perez et al., 2000.

claim: A model based on the Price equation predicts that mtDNA bottleneck should facilitate partner fidelity feedback at the corresponding level.
source: A model based on the Price equation predicts that mtDNA bottleneck (inheriting a small number of mtDNAs per mitochondrion or per germ cell) should facilitate PFF at the corresponding level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Price equation framework.

claim: mtDNA bottleneck has been observed during fly and mammalian oogenesis.
source: Indeed, mtDNA bottleneck has been observed during fly and mammalian oogenesis (Koehler et al., 1991; Chinnery et al., 2000; Cree et al., 2008; Hill et al., 2014) (Appendix note 27).
evidence: Supported by citations to Koehler et al., 1991; Chinnery et al., 2000; Cree et al., 2008; and Hill et al., 2014.

claim: mtDNA bottleneck means that oocytes from a mother heteroplasmic for functional and dysfunctional mtDNAs will exhibit high variability in the frequency of functional mtDNAs that they inherit.
source: This mtDNA bottleneck means that oocytes from a mother heteroplasmic for functional and dysfunctional mtDNAs will exhibit high variability in the frequency of functional mtDNAs that they inherit.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequence of mtDNA bottleneck.

claim: Oocytes dominated by dysfunctional mtDNAs can be purged via apoptosis, creating a germline mtDNA filter that improves the prognosis of offspring.
source: Oocytes dominated by dysfunctional mtDNAs can be subsequently purged via apoptosis (Appendix note 28), thus creating a germline mtDNA filter that improves the prognosis of offspring.
evidence: This is an inference combining multiple mechanisms discussed earlier.

claim: Partner fidelity feedback and partner choice can operate on organismal or sub-organismal entities.
source: I have revised the definitions of PC and PFF so that they are orthogonal and so that they can operate on organismal or sub-organismal entities.
evidence: This is a summary of the author's theoretical contribution.

claim: Partner fidelity feedback suppresses cheaters that have escaped partner choice via repeated interactions between entities in groups that show high variability in cooperator frequency.
source: PFF suppresses cheaters that have escaped PC (if PC exists) via repeated interactions between entities in groups that, by chance, show high variability in cooperator frequency.
evidence: This is part of the revised definition of PFF proposed by the author.

claim: Partner fidelity feedback and partner choice can act in conjunction at multiple levels to promote cooperation, as exemplified in the mitochondrion-eukaryote cooperation.
source: PFF and PC can also act in conjunction at multiple levels to promote cooperation, as exemplified in the mitochondrion-eukaryote cooperation.
evidence: This is a synthesis inference from the analysis of mitochondrion-eukaryote cooperation.
